assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 600 requests/s at peak against a shared MCP server: 10% tools/list (capability discovery on client connect), 65% fast tool calls, 25% long-running tool calls handed to a worker.

assumptions.subject: architecture
assumptions.statement: The MODEL is deliberately not part of this design. In MCP the model runs on the client side (Claude Desktop, an IDE, an agent host) and this server only answers JSON-RPC tool requests, so there is no model provider, no token spend and no LLM component to size. That is the correct MCP shape, not an omission.

assumptions.subject: mcp
assumptions.statement: 400 req/s per MCP server instance: JSON-RPC parse, JSON-Schema validation of tool arguments and dispatch on 2 vCPU.

assumptions.subject: worker
assumptions.statement: 40 tasks/s per worker instance. A long tool call (HTTP fetch, sandboxed execution) is I/O bound at roughly 2 s with about 80 concurrent slots per instance.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Every fast path checks the cache; 35% of fast tool calls miss and read the database. Async calls always write a result row.

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: Egress is billed per response: ~8 KB per tool manifest, ~4 KB per fast tool result, ~2 KB for the async acknowledgement.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The write primary is a SINGLE instance and the engine reports it as a single point of failure. That is the shape of the design: high availability comes from Multi-AZ standby failover, which v1 cannot express - `instances` means active capacity, and a warm standby serves no traffic. Budget for it (the RDS price band tops out at Multi-AZ) and treat the SPOF flag as a reminder, not a modelling error.

assumptions.subject: engine
assumptions.statement: Streamable-HTTP/SSE sessions are modelled as request/response. The v1 engine has no long-lived-connection primitive, so per-connection memory and the concurrency ceiling of held SSE streams are NOT captured, and those are usually what breaks an MCP server first.

_library.summary: A production MCP server: tool discovery, fast tool calls, and a queue plus workers for the slow ones.
